articles.title: Singing in the Mud
articles.dek: A Navy admiral once told a stadium of graduates about the night a class of shivering trainees began to sing. James, the brother of Jesus, had already written the same song into the first lines of his letter.
articles.quote: Joy, in James's vocabulary, is a verdict you reach about what God is building in you, long before you can see the walls go up.
articles.body:
The sun was going down over the Tijuana sloughs, a stretch of swampy ground near the border between San Diego and Mexico, and a class of young Navy SEAL trainees was sinking into the mud. It was Wednesday of Hell Week, six days of brutal training with almost no sleep, and for some small offense the instructors had ordered the whole class into the muck. The cold mud rose until nothing showed above it but their heads. Then the instructors made an offer: if just five men would quit, everyone could climb out and get warm.

Years later, Admiral William McRaven, by then the commander of all U.S. Special Operations forces, told this story to the graduating class of the University of Texas at Austin on May 17, 2014. He remembered looking around and seeing that some of the men were close to giving up. Eight more hours of darkness stood between them and sunrise, and the chattering of teeth was so loud it was hard to hear anything else. Then one voice began to sing. McRaven said the song was terribly out of tune but sung with great enthusiasm, and soon a second voice joined it, and before long the entire class was singing in the mud. The instructors threatened more time in the cold if the singing continued, and the singing continued anyway. McRaven told the graduates that somehow the mud seemed a little warmer and the dawn not so far away. He closed the story with a line that has traveled around the world ever since: "If you want to change the world, start singing when you're up to your neck in mud."

Nearly two thousand years earlier, a man named James wrote a letter to people who were up to their necks in a different kind of mud. James was the brother of Jesus (Galatians 1:19), raised in the same small house in Nazareth, and for years he did not believe his older brother was anyone special (John 7:5). Then the risen Jesus appeared to him personally (1 Corinthians 15:7), and the skeptic became the leader of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13). Yet when he sat down to write, he claimed no family privilege at all. He introduced himself simply as "James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" (James 1:1).

He addressed his letter "to the twelve tribes scattered among the nations" (James 1:1). The Greek word behind "scattered" is diaspora, a farming word for seed flung across a field. Many of these believers had been driven out of Jerusalem when persecution broke out after Stephen's death (Acts 8:1; 11:19). Reading the rest of the letter, we meet the conditions they lived in. Rich men dragged them into court (James 2:6), employers held back the wages of their workers (James 5:4), and some had no clothes or daily food (James 2:15). These were displaced, underpaid people far from home, and Filipinos who have watched a loved one board a plane for Riyadh or Dubai will recognize them immediately.

To people in that situation, James writes his very first instruction. He skips the warm-up and goes straight into the cold water:

"Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance. Let perseverance finish its work so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything." (James 1:2–4)

At first hearing, this can sound almost cruel, as if James were asking hurting people to smile through their pain. The key is the verb he chose. "Consider" translates the Greek hēgēsasthe, a word for weighing matters carefully and reaching a settled judgment. Paul uses the same word when he writes, "I consider everything a loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8). James is asking for a conclusion of the mind, and he gives the evidence in the same breath: "because you know." Joy, in James's vocabulary, is a verdict you reach about what God is building in you, long before you can see the walls go up.

The thing being built has a name. "Perseverance" is the Greek hypomonē, made from two small words, hypo (under) and menō (to remain). It describes a person who remains under a heavy load without slipping out from beneath it. Those trainees in the sloughs were living a picture of the word, staying under the mud through the long hours until morning. James even gives perseverance a job description. "Let perseverance finish its work," he says, as though it were a skilled craftsman who needs to be allowed to complete the house. The result is a believer who is teleios, mature and grown up, and holoklēros, a word for something whole in every part, with no piece missing.

Then James does something lovely with his words. He ends verse 4 with the phrase "not lacking anything," and he begins verse 5 with the same Greek verb: "If any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to you" (James 1:5). One way to read the connection is this. James knows that the person in the middle of the trial rarely feels complete. They feel short of strength, short of answers, and short of any idea what to do next. So he points them immediately to a Father who gives generously and never scolds the one who asks. The same God who allows the testing also supplies the wisdom to walk through it, because "every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, who does not change like shifting shadows" (James 1:17).

This is where the night in the mud becomes so moving. The first song left the water every bit as cold, yet it gave the night a new meaning. The men began to hear themselves as a class that would make it to dawn together. James was offering his scattered friends that same new hearing of their own story. Their trials were real and painful, and he never pretended otherwise. He simply told them what the pain was producing, and that knowledge allowed them to sing before the sun came up.

James had lived this himself. He had watched his own brother die on a Roman cross, and he had spent that dark Saturday believing, like everyone else, that the story was over. Then came the morning when Jesus stood before him alive. A man who has seen that kind of sunrise can write with confidence, "Blessed is the one who perseveres under trial because, having stood the test, that person will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love him" (James 1:12).

Perhaps you are in the mud this morning. It may be a hospital bill that keeps growing, a marriage that has gone quiet, a board exam result that broke your heart, or the long loneliness of working abroad for people you only see on a phone screen. James does not ask you to pretend the cold is warm. He invites you to reach a verdict about it. Before the day gets busy, you could take a scrap of paper and finish this sentence honestly: "With God's help, this trial is producing ____ in me." Then, in the same prayer, ask for the wisdom you lack, trusting that God gives it generously and without a frown.

And consider singing. Filipinos have always known how to sing in hard places, at wakes, in evacuation centers, and in crowded dormitories far from home. Choose one song of faith that you love and sing it aloud today, even badly, even with a shaking voice. You may discover what McRaven's class discovered, that one voice gives courage to another. Somewhere near you is a person who is sinking and close to quitting, and James ends this chapter by reminding us to look after those "in their distress" (James 1:27). Your song might be the first note they hear.

The dawn is closer than it feels. Perseverance is still at work in you, finishing what God started, and the Father of lights has a crown of life waiting for those who remain under the load out of love for him. So stay in the mud a little longer, and when you are ready, start the song.

articles.title: The Cells at the Edge of the Wound
articles.dek: In one of the Bible's darkest chapters, God searched a whole city for a single person to stand in a broken wall. His search shows how families and friendships are mended, and who is closest to the break.
articles.quote: Every breach God has ever mended began with one person willing to stand at its edge.
articles.body:
Scrape a thin line through a layer of living skin cells growing in a laboratory dish, and you have made a wound in miniature. Biologists do this on purpose. They call it a scratch assay, and it is one of the simplest ways to watch healing happen. Under the microscope, the cells along both edges of the empty strip begin to change within hours. They flatten and stretch, push thin, ruffled sheets of membrane out toward the open space, and slowly the whole border starts to creep forward into the gap.

In 2007 a team of physicists and biologists at the Institut Curie in Paris filmed this process closely and saw something lovely. Certain cells at the very edge take the lead. These "leader cells" grow larger and more active than their neighbors and crawl out into the gap first. The cells behind them stay linked to them by molecular handholds called cadherins, so they follow in like a line of people holding hands across a stream. When the two advancing edges finally meet in the middle, the cells sense one another and stop, a behavior scientists call contact inhibition. The tissue is whole again, and the cells that mended it were the ones standing nearest the break. Your own body did a version of this the last time you scraped your knee.

Twenty-six centuries ago, God went looking for someone like that. The prophet Ezekiel was a priest who had been carried off to Babylon in 597 BC with the first wave of exiles. From a refugee settlement by the Kebar River, he spoke to his fellow captives about the city they had left behind. Jerusalem was still standing, and many exiles were sure they would soon go home to it, but Ezekiel could see that it was rotting from within.

The chapters in today's reading are among the hardest in his book. In chapter 21 the Lord describes a sword "sharpened and polished" (Ezekiel 21:9), then pictures the king of Babylon standing at a fork in the road, shaking arrows and consulting idols to decide whether to march on Ammon or on Jerusalem (21:21–22). The lot falls on Jerusalem. Ezekiel is told to groan in front of the people "with broken heart and bitter grief" (21:6), so that when they ask him why, he can tell them what is coming. God's messenger was asked to feel the grief before he announced it, which tells us something about the God who sent him.

Chapter 22 reads like a prosecutor's list of charges against the city, and what stands out is how personal they are. "In you they have treated father and mother with contempt; in you they have oppressed the foreigner and mistreated the fatherless and the widow" (22:7). Neighbors extort neighbors for profit (22:12). Near the end, the Lord walks through every level of society. The princes are "like a roaring lion tearing its prey" (22:25), and the priests blur the line between holy and common (22:26). Officials are "like wolves" (22:27), prophets whitewash it all with false visions (22:28), and the ordinary people of the land "oppress the poor and needy" (22:29). Then comes what may be the saddest sentence in the whole book.

"I looked for someone among them who would build up the wall and stand before me in the gap on behalf of the land so I would not have to destroy it, but I found no one." (Ezekiel 22:30)

The picture comes from siege warfare, and every listener would have understood it at once. The Hebrew word for wall, gader, means a stone fence or wall, the kind built around a vineyard or a town. The word for gap, perets, means a breach, a place where the wall has been broken through. In an ancient siege, attackers battered one section until it gave way, and the life of the whole city then depended on whether defenders would rush to that single opening and hold it with their bodies while others piled stones behind them. Ezekiel had already used this image against the false prophets of his day: "You have not gone up to the breaches in the wall to repair it" (13:5). Psalm 106:23 remembers Moses the same way, saying God would have destroyed his people "had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him."

Ezekiel 22:30 is a verdict, and it is also a window into God's heart. The Lord is the one doing the searching. He wanted a reason to spare the city, and he looked for one before the judgment fell. The search was also strikingly small. The Hebrew asks for ish, a single person, one man or woman willing to step into one breach. One faithful life, standing before God on behalf of others, was the very thing he was hoping to find.

Look again at the charges in verses 7 through 12, and you will see that most of the breaches were relational. People despised their parents, abandoned widows and cheated their neighbors. Babylon's battering rams broke Jerusalem's walls in 586 BC, but by Ezekiel's account the city had been breached long before, in households and marketplaces, wherever people stopped caring for one another. That suggests the repair would have been relational too: a son honoring his aging father, a merchant weighing his rice honestly, a family taking in a widow. As in the dish under the microscope, the ones best placed to mend a wound are those standing nearest to it.

The Bible does not leave that empty search as its final word. Isaiah describes the same scene and then goes further: "He saw that there was no one, he was appalled that there was no one to intervene; so his own arm achieved salvation for him" (Isaiah 59:16). Christians have long seen this fulfilled in Jesus, who stepped into the breach between God and us with his own body. Hebrews 7:25 says he "always lives to intercede" for those who come to God through him. Because Christ holds the great gap, we can step into the smaller ones around us freely, with nothing left to prove.

Most of us know someone who has stood in the gap for our own family. Often it is the tita who still calls the two brothers who stopped speaking after the land dispute, or the lola who has prayed for years for the grandchild who drifted away from church. Families rarely stay whole by accident. They are held together by people who walk toward the break when everyone else is walking away from it.

You may be the person nearest to a gap right now. It might be a sibling you have not spoken to since the last burol, or a friend whose long silence you have quietly read as rejection. Leader cells move slowly, a fraction of a millimeter a day, and they never close a wound alone; they move forward while holding on to the cells behind them. Standing in the gap usually begins in a similar way, with a short message that says, "I've been thinking about you," or a visit with a bag of warm pandesal and no speech prepared. It also includes prayer, which is what "stand before me" in verse 30 implies. The one in the breach faces God on behalf of the people on the other side.

Ezekiel's generation heard the hardest words a prophet ever carried: "I found no one." Your story can be different. Every breach God has ever mended began with one person willing to stand at its edge. Choose the gap closest to you this week, ask the Lord to steady you, and take a single step toward it, holding on to Christ and to anyone willing to walk with you. God is still searching for someone, and he is glad when he finds you there.

articles.title: The Promise That Passed the Fire
articles.dek: Every year in London, a jury of goldsmiths melts down the nation's coins to see if they are true. A tired, overlooked psalm writer said God's promises had already passed a harder test.
articles.quote: A promise you have watched come through the fire is a promise you can learn to love.
articles.body:
Every year, usually in February, a jury of goldsmiths gathers in a grand old hall in the City of London to do something that has been done, in one form or another, for more than seven hundred years. In front of them sit coins pulled at random from the Royal Mint's production over the past year. The ceremony is called the Trial of the Pyx, after the boxwood chest, the pyx, in which the sample coins were once locked away. The jurors count the coins and weigh them, and then send them to be assayed, which means melted and chemically tested to see whether the metal inside is what the Crown says it is. Some weeks later the verdict is read aloud before an official who still carries the lovely old title of the King's Remembrancer.

It looks like pageantry, and partly it is. The reason behind it, though, is very plain. A coin is a promise stamped in metal, and the people who use it need to know that the promise is true. In the Middle Ages, rulers short of money were tempted to stretch their silver with cheaper metals, and it was ordinary people who paid for the cheating. So England built a ritual that put the promise into the fire and let the metal speak for itself. The coins that pass carry their word with a quiet confidence that centuries of testing have earned.

Most Filipinos have seen a smaller version of this at the counter of a sanglaan, a pawnshop. A mother brings in her wedding ring the week before tuition is due. The appraiser rubs it across a small black stone, puts a drop of acid on the gold streak, and watches. He takes no one's word for it, and she takes no offense, because everyone in the shop understands the rule. Gold is trusted once it has been tested.

Psalm 119 was written by someone who understood that rule from the inside. It is the longest chapter in the Bible, 176 verses, built as an acrostic: twenty-two stanzas of eight lines each, one stanza for every letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with every line in a stanza beginning with the same letter. The writer is never named. What we do know about him comes from his own words scattered through the psalm. Arrogant people mock him (Psalm 119:51). Rulers persecute him without cause (Psalm 119:161). He describes himself as "like a wineskin in the smoke" (Psalm 119:83), dried out and cracking from hanging too long near the fire.

By the eighteenth stanza, the one built on the letter tsadhe, he is tired, and he says so honestly. "My zeal wears me out, for my enemies ignore your words" (Psalm 119:139). He has cared about God's ways for so long, and watched so many people shrug at them, that the caring itself has worn him thin. He adds, "Though I am lowly and despised, I do not forget your precepts" (Psalm 119:141). The word for lowly, tsa'ir, is the word Hebrew uses for the youngest or the smallest, the one at the end of the line whom nobody consults. Then comes the plainest sentence of all: "Trouble and distress have come upon me" (Psalm 119:143). In the middle of this weary, overlooked stretch of his life, he writes a line that sounds as if it came from the assay room.

"Your promises have been thoroughly tested, and your servant loves them." (Psalm 119:140, NIV)

The phrase "thoroughly tested" translates a Hebrew word, tseruphah, from the verb tsaraph, which belongs to the metalworker's shop. It means to smelt, to refine, to put silver in the furnace until the impurities burn away. Malachi uses the same verb when he pictures God sitting "as a refiner and purifier of silver" (Malachi 3:3). Another psalm says it outright: "And the words of the LORD are flawless, like silver purified in a crucible, like gold refined seven times" (Psalm 12:6). The word for "promises" here, 'imrah, means something spoken, a word said aloud. So the psalmist is saying that what God has spoken has gone through the smelter and come out pure.

Where, then, did the testing happen? One way to read this stanza is that the furnace was the writer's own life. The weariness of verse 139 and the contempt of verse 141 and the distress of verse 143 were the heat, and God's word was the metal placed in it. He is speaking as someone who has watched it from close range. He leaned his full weight on what God said during the years when nobody respected him, and it held. The verb he chooses afterward is love, the same ordinary, warm Hebrew word, 'ahav, used for Jacob's love for Rachel. People tend to love most deeply the friend who stayed through their worst year, and this writer feels that way about God's promises. A promise you have watched come through the fire is a promise you can learn to love.

The shape of the poem carries a gentle message of its own. Because every line of the stanza must begin with tsadhe, the writer opens with tsaddiq, "You are righteous, LORD" (Psalm 119:137), and closes with tsedeq, "Your statutes are always righteous" (Psalm 119:144). The word for trouble in verse 143, tsar, begins with the very same letter. His distress is written into the same alphabet as God's righteousness and sits right between its opening and closing lines. This suggests that the hard season he describes was held the whole time inside the faithfulness of God, enclosed on both sides by it, even when he felt small and spent.

Many readers know what verse 141 feels like. Perhaps you are the one in the family whose sacrifices go unmentioned, or the worker abroad whose name the employer never quite learns, or the believer in an office where faith earns a polite smile and nothing more. The psalm gives no promise that this feeling will disappear by Friday. What it offers is the testimony of someone who stood in the same place and found that God's word kept its weight. The writer's own smallness became the furnace where he learned what God's promises are made of.

There is a detail from those London goldsmiths worth borrowing. For centuries, silver brought to their hall for testing was stamped with a small mark once it passed, and that is where the English word hallmark comes from. You can make a hallmark of your own. Think back over a hard season you have already come through, and find one thing God said that held for you then. It might be "Never will I leave you; never will I forsake you" (Hebrews 13:5), or "My grace is sufficient for you" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Write it in the margin of your Bible or on the first page of a notebook, and beside it write the year it was tested and a few words about what happened. On a heavier day, that small note will remind you that this promise has already passed through your own fire.

The stanza ends with a prayer short enough to carry all day: "Give me understanding that I may live" (Psalm 119:144). The psalmist does not ask for his troubles to be explained or his critics to be silenced. He asks to understand God's word deeply enough to keep living by it, and that request is open to anyone who feels worn out and small this week. The promises you are leaning on have been in the fire before, in the lives of countless people who went ahead of you, and they came out pure. You can put your full weight on them today and keep a record of how they hold.

articles.title: The House That Walked Across the Field
articles.dek: A bayanihan crew can carry a whole nipa house on its shoulders. Proverbs 24 asks a quieter question: who is holding your poles, and what fills the rooms inside?
articles.quote: Envy stares at a neighbor's gate; wisdom tends the rooms no one can see from the road.
articles.body:
On a dry morning in a barrio, the men of the neighborhood gather around a small bahay kubo. A family has bought a lot on the other side of the rice field, and in the old Filipino way, nobody calls for a truck. Long bamboo poles are slid beneath the floor beams and lashed tight with rope. A dozen men, sometimes twenty, take their places, crouch low, and on a shouted count lift the whole house onto their shoulders, and the house begins to walk.

Anyone who has seen it, or seen the familiar picture of it on a school wall or an old calendar, remembers the details. The men move in a slow shuffle so the walls will not sway. Children run ahead to kick stones out of the path, and somebody's tito calls the rhythm so every foot falls together. At the new lot the women are already waiting with rice, pancit, and cold drinks, because a bayanihan always ends at a shared table. No one is paid. The wage is the meal and the unspoken promise that when your turn comes, these same shoulders will be under your floor.

The word comes from bayan, the town or community, and it names something deeper than a clever way to move a house. A house can only travel like this when the people holding the poles can be trusted. If a few of those men decided halfway across the field that the job was no longer worth their trouble, the house would tilt, and everything inside would spill into the mud. The whole thing rises or falls on who is underneath it.

That picture sits close to one of the plainest and most hopeful passages in Proverbs. Chapter 24 belongs to a section the book itself calls the "sayings of the wise" (Proverbs 22:17), a collection of short lessons gathered to train young people for responsible life at home, at work, and at the city gate. Many scholars point out that parts of this section resemble an older Egyptian teaching called the Instruction of Amenemope. Israel's teachers clearly knew the wisdom of their neighbors, yet they anchored every lesson in a single purpose, stated at the very start: "So that your trust may be in the LORD" (Proverbs 22:19).

Within this short collection, the teacher warns against envy three separate times (Proverbs 23:17; 24:1; 24:19). A good teacher repeats a lesson when students keep failing it, and envy is a lesson every generation fails. Here is how chapter 24 opens: "Do not envy the wicked, do not desire their company; for their hearts plot violence, and their lips talk about making trouble" (Proverbs 24:1–2). The Hebrew word behind "violence" is shod, which means ruin or devastation, the kind of damage that leaves a place stripped. The people this young reader is tempted to admire are, at heart, planning destruction.

Then, with no transition at all, the teacher writes this:

"By wisdom a house is built, and through understanding it is established; through knowledge its rooms are filled with rare and beautiful treasures." (Proverbs 24:3–4)

The two pictures are placed side by side on purpose. Verse 2 shows hearts that plan ruin, and verse 3 shows hands that build. One way to read the passage is that the envy question is really a building question. Whatever we envy, we slowly begin to imitate, and whoever we imitate becomes the architect of our life. The proverb is asking what kind of house you are putting up, and whose methods you are borrowing to do it.

Most of us have felt the pull. There is the neighbor whose house went up in a single year, with a gate taller than anyone else's, while everyone quietly wonders where the money came from. There is the former classmate whose life on Facebook looks like a permanent vacation, built, we later learn, on shortcuts and on people left behind. Envy whispers that they are ahead and we are foolish for moving so slowly. The proverb answers by asking us to look past the gate to the heart, and Proverbs 14:11 finishes the thought: "The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish." A house built on ruin eventually becomes a ruin.

The building words in verses 3 and 4 reward a closer look. The house is "built" (banah), then "established" (kun, a word for setting something firm and upright so it will not topple), then "filled" (male). In Hebrew, bayit, "house," meant both the structure and the household, the walls and the family living inside them. And the word for "rooms" (chadarim) refers to the inner chambers, the private spaces at the back of the home where visitors rarely go. The treasures the proverb praises are stored where the passing world cannot see them. The wicked person's house is designed to impress from the road, while the wise person's house grows rich in the rooms that matter: a marriage that keeps its promises, children who trust their parents' word, a quiet table where grace is said and meant.

Here the gospel steps in, because honest readers know their own envy too well. We have desired the company of people who were tearing things down, and we have borrowed their shortcuts more than once. If building a household depends on our wisdom alone, the poles slip from our hands. Proverbs itself pictures Wisdom as one who "has built her house" (Proverbs 9:1), and the New Testament gives that Wisdom a name. Paul writes that Christ Jesus "has become for us wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:30), and he describes Christ as the one "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). The very words of our proverb, wisdom, knowledge, and treasure, gather around a person.

Jesus also told a story about two builders, and the wise one is the person who "hears these words of mine and puts them into practice" (Matthew 7:24). Better still, Hebrews says of believers, "we are his house" (Hebrews 3:6). The house we could not build he builds, and the weight we could not carry he takes on his own shoulders, the way a neighbor slides under the bamboo pole and lifts. "Unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain" (Psalm 127:1), and the good news is that he has pledged himself to the work.

That makes the practical side of Proverbs 24 gentler and more hopeful. When envy rises today, at a neighbor's renovation or a stranger's highlight reel, you can pause long enough to ask what that person's heart may be planning and what you would have to become to get what they have. Very often the honest answer will cool the envy on the spot. Then you can turn your attention back to your own inner rooms and place one treasure there before the day ends, perhaps an apology you have been delaying or an hour with your children with the phones set aside. Verse 1 also asks you to choose your company with care, so consider who is holding the poles of your life, and thank God for the trustworthy ones.

Every household eventually has to move across some field: a sickness, a job lost, a child leaving, old age arriving at the door. On that day the height of the gate will not matter much. What will matter is who is under the poles and what fills the rooms. Envy stares at a neighbor's gate; wisdom tends the rooms no one can see from the road. Tend yours today, slowly and faithfully, and trust the One whose shoulders are already beneath your floor.
